text: Building a working REST Message follows a real, specific order, and skipping ahead is exactly how configuration mistakes end up buried inside script bugs much later, where they're far harder to diagnose. Let's walk the three steps in the order they actually need to happen.

First, configure the parent record once: the base Endpoint, entered exactly as the provider documents it, and the Authentication Profile every Function will inherit by default. Second, add a Function for each real operation you actually need — don't build Functions speculatively for operations nothing calls yet. Third, test each Function before you ever write a line of script against it.

Two Functions under the same parent can look very different from each other. A GET operation, like looking up a customer by email, just needs a query-string placeholder in its relative path, nothing more. A POST operation, like creating a customer, needs its own Content-Type header and a JSON body template with its own placeholders — dollar sign, curly braces, name — ready for script to fill in before the request goes out.

Every Function has a real, built-in Test capability sitting right on the form. You supply values for whatever placeholders it defines, and ServiceNow sends an actual live HTTP request to the real external system — this is not a simulation of any kind. The test results show the real HTTP status code and the real response body the external system actually sent back.

Read the status code to know exactly where to look next. A 401 means the Authentication Profile is wrong or stale. A 404 usually means the relative path, or the base Endpoint underneath it, is wrong. A 500 means the external system itself errored on its end, not your configuration at all.

Testing at the record level isolates configuration problems from script problems before they ever get tangled together. A clean 200 here means any later failure you hit from script is a script-side bug, not a configuration one hiding underneath it.
